DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The case for a price rise is reasonable, but the document has a factual error about the risotto, leaves the beef cost increase out of the projection, and relies on an untested assumption that volumes will hold. I'd fix these before it goes to the owners.

## Errors that affect the recommendation

**1. The risotto is the highest-margin dish, not the weakest (5.2).**
Table 1 shows risotto at 80%, the best on the menu, and £11.20 gross profit per plate, which is more than the burger (£10.80) and curry (£10.90). Its 90 plates a week is tied with specials, not clearly the lowest. The case for removal as written contradicts the paper's own data. If there is a real reason, such as kitchen complexity, waste or a plan for the replacement special, it needs to be stated. The paper should also say what the replacement's food cost will be, since "same price" says nothing about margin. Dropping the only listed vegetarian main is a risk in itself.

**2. The projection ignores the 12% beef increase (sections 4 and 5.3).**
The £810 a week and £42,120 a year figures are arithmetically correct (310 + 260 + 240 = £810, × 52), but they use today's food costs. Beef affects the burger and steak, so these are the worst-case cost increases, assuming the whole plate cost is beef:
- Burger: +£0.50 per plate × 260 = about £131 a week
- Steak: +£1.25 per plate × 120 = about £150 a week

That cuts the gain to roughly £530 a week, or about £27,500 a year, at the low end. The true figure lies between that and £42,000, depending on how much of each plate's cost is beef. Post-rise margins fall to about 70.6% for the burger and 58.4% for the steak, so the steak ends up below its current 60% even after the increase. The "about 71%" main-course margin is also overstated. Using the table's figures and assuming specials average around £18, I get roughly 69-70% now and about 70.7% after the increases, before beef. With beef costs it is closer to 68-69%, so the increases would not restore the 70% target on their own. Specials may also contain beef.

**3. "Six trading days a week" (section 8).**
Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five days.

## Weak reasoning

- **Volume assumption.** "Volumes will hold" is the main driver of the £42k and is asserted, not tested. The increases are about 6.1% (fish), 6.7% (burger) and 7.7% (steak). A sensitivity table would help, for example showing the result if those three dishes lose 3%, 5% or 10% of plates.
- **Evidence from 2024.** It cites "no visible effect on bookings", but bookings are not plates sold per dish or spend per cover. It also doesn't say how large that increase was.
- **Loyal customer base.** The 60% repeat share cuts both ways, because regulars are the guests most likely to notice a price change.
- **Lunch trade.** "A small share of main-course sales" is unsupported. Only Friday and Saturday dinner (just under half) is quantified, so the lunch split should be given.
- **Competitor positioning.** The "below the midpoint" claim checks out for all three dishes. But the new fish and chips price (£17.50) moves above the cheapest competitor's £16.95, so "lowest in the group" no longer holds for it. Five menus is also a small sample.
- **Monitoring (section 6).** Comparing spring sales with a January-February baseline will mix price effects with seasonal changes. The beef cost change also lands on the same date, so the paper should say what triggers a rollback.

## Smaller points

- Section 1 gives an overall food margin of 67% against a 70% target, but the paper only analyses mains. It should state the mains-only margin today (about 69-70% by my estimate) so readers can see how much of the gap mains can close.
- Specials (90 plates, "various" price) are the one line where revenue can't be reconstructed, so any margin calculation involves an assumption.
- Not drawing attention to the increases on the menu is fine, but staff should have an answer ready for guests who ask.

## Suggested fixes

1. Correct the risotto rationale, or drop 5.2 or support it with other evidence.
2. Rebuild 5.3 with post-1 April food costs, showing a range for the beef share of plate cost.
3. Consider whether the steak needs a larger rise, or a different cut or portion, to keep its margin.
4. Add a volume sensitivity table and a rollback trigger.
5. Correct "six trading days" to five.

I can redo the projection in a table with beef costs and volume scenarios if you'd like.
